general_notes.general_notes:
This study applied normative modeling to Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS), formerly known as benign Rolandic epilepsy, which is the most common pediatric focal epilepsy. SeLECTS is characterized by age-dependent onset (3-14 years, peak at 7 years) and remission after adolescence. The study utilized the CentileBrain framework (Ge et al. 2024), which provides systematic empirical benchmarking for normative modeling of brain morphometric measures. The normative models were sex-specific. Multivariable fractional polynomial regression was chosen because it can determine the functional form of predictors by testing a wide family of shapes and multiple turning points while providing good fit at the extremes of covariates. Cognitive assessments included Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (measuring analog perception, reasoning, and abstract abilities) and Integrated Visual and Auditory Continuous Performance Test (IVACPT, screening tool for ADHD). Only 75 of 187 children with SeLECTS received cognitive assessments. Clinical information (duration of illness, duration of medicine, dose of medicine, seizure frequency) had some missing data as indicated by footnote in Table 1. All participants had negative presentations on conventional structural MRI. The study received ethics approval from Jinling Hospital (ID: 2018NZKY-020-02) and Institute of Psychology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IDs: H15001, H15045, H22068). The devCCNP datasets are publicly available at https://www.scidb.cn/en/detail?dataSetId=c81f0e90a51b4cfca348ce4da6ca734e. The raw case-control data are available on request from corresponding author. Structural MRI was acquired on Siemens Trio Tim 3.0 Tesla scanner using magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo sequence (TR/TE=2300/2.98ms, flip angle=9°, FOV=256×256mm², matrix=256×256, slice thickness=1mm, no gap, 176 slices). The paper was received November 20, 2024, revised February 17, 2025, and accepted February 23, 2025.

- deviation_metric: "Z-score calculated as z = (Y - Ŷ) / σ where Y is observed value, Ŷ is predicted value from normative model, and σ is predicted standard deviation. Regional non-normal z-scores defined as infra-normal (z < -1.96, 5th percentile) or supra-normal (z > 1.96, 95th percentile). Percentage of participants with infra-normal or supra-normal deviations calculated for each region. Number of regions with abnormal deviations counted per participant. Averaged normative deviation computed for each morphometric measure type."
- association_analysis: "Group comparisons of percentage of participants with abnormal deviations conducted using 2-proportion z-test. Group comparisons of normative z-scores and observed measures using two-sample t-test. Association between number of regions with infra- or supra-normal deviations and clinical manifestations examined using Spearman correlation. Association between averaged deviations of each morphometric measure and clinical manifestations examined using Pearson's correlation. Clinical variables tested: duration of disease, seizure frequency, Raven's total score (cognitive measure), duration of medicine, dose of medicine. False discovery rate (FDR) correction applied for multiple comparisons. Significance threshold P < 0.05. Support vector classification (SVC) models with linear kernel and 5-fold cross-validation used to compare predictive performance of normative deviations vs. observed morphometric measures for diagnostic classification, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) as performance metric."
- key_findings_brief: "Children with SeLECTS showed similar distributions of brain morphometric normative deviations to healthy controls, with only a few extreme deviations in a minority of individuals, and the number of regions with deviations correlated with disease duration, seizure frequency, and cognitive function."
- key_findings_detailed: "The distributions of z-scores for regional subcortical volume, cortical thickness, and surface area were highly overlapping between SeLECTS and control groups. For subcortical volume, infra-normal deviations ranged from 1.6% to 8.6% in SeLECTS vs. 0.9% to 4.6% in controls; supra-normal deviations ranged from 2.7% to 7.5% in SeLECTS vs. 1.9% to 6.5% in controls. For cortical thickness, infra-normal deviations ranged from 1.1% to 11.8% in SeLECTS vs. 0.9% to 9.3% in controls; supra-normal deviations ranged from 0.5% to 13.9% in both groups. For surface area, infra-normal deviations ranged from 0.5% to 13.4% in SeLECTS vs. 0.9% to 13.0% in controls; supra-normal deviations ranged from 1.1% to 9.6% in SeLECTS vs. 0.9% to 10.2% in controls. No significant group differences were found in the percentage of participants with regional infra- or supra-normal z-scores for any individual brain region after FDR correction. However, when examining the overall proportion of participants with any infra-normal deviations in subcortical volume, children with SeLECTS (34.2%) showed significantly higher rates than controls (18.5%) (χ²=7.54, P=0.04 with FDR correction). For cortical thickness, 86.1% of SeLECTS vs. 77.8% of controls had infra-normal deviations (not significant); for surface area, 82.4% of SeLECTS vs. 74.1% of controls (not significant). The number of regions with supra-normal deviations in subcortical volume was positively correlated with duration of disease (R²=0.06, P=0.05) and seizure frequency (R²=0.11, P=0.01). The number of regions with infra-normal deviations in cortical thickness was positively correlated with Raven's total score (R²=0.07, P=0.05). The averaged regional z-scores of surface area were positively correlated with seizure frequency (R²=0.06, P=0.001). Almost all participants had averaged normative deviations within the normal distribution (only one child with SeLECTS exhibited averaged supra-normal deviation in surface area). Support vector classification using regional z-scores achieved AUC=0.56, while observed morphometric measures achieved AUC=0.48 for diagnostic classification, both showing poor discrimination."
- key_limitations: "First, the study could benefit from inclusion of a larger sample of children, which would result in more stable and generalizable normative models. Second, the morphometric measures were based on cross-sectional data and did not capture longitudinal changes; studies have shown that cross-sectional models and brain measures may underestimate the extent of age-related brain changes. Third, the model only considers sex and age, and demographic, developmental, and lifestyle factors were not included in the analysis."
- application_notes: "The study emphasizes the value of normative modeling in revealing individual-level heterogeneity that may not be detected in traditional case-control comparisons. The lack of strong statistically significant differences between epilepsy cases and controls suggests that changes may occur at the level of cortical microcircuits. The authors note that the limited sample size of abnormal subjects may diminish effects in group comparisons. The study offers a new explanation for controversial results in the literature from the perspective of individual heterogeneity. The authors suggest that monitoring brain abnormalities throughout the course of disease is important given that extreme distributions of heterogeneous brain morphometric deviations are present in a minority of individuals. Future work should incorporate longitudinal and cross-modal data, and consider additional demographic, developmental, and lifestyle factors in normative model training and application."
